claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by sluggish atomic diffusion and surface segregation of oxygen-affine constituents.
High configurational entropy intrinsically causes sluggish atomic diffusion.
Sluggish atomic diffusion retards grain growth.
Sluggish atomic diffusion retards phase separation.
High-oxygen-affinity constituents such as Al or Cr thermodynamically segregate to the nanoalloy surface.
Surface-segregated Al or Cr rapidly forms a uniform, self-healing passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer protects the nanoalloy against further oxidation.
High-entropy nanoalloys produced by bottom-up synthesis typically have grain sizes of 20–50 nm.
Suppressed grain-boundary mobility is caused by sluggish atomic diffusion.
Under oxidative conditions, slow diffusion permits selective segregation of high-oxygen-affinity elements to the surface.
Selective surface segregation facilitates rapid formation of a protective passive oxide.
The protective oxide limits oxygen penetration and chemical degradation.
After high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less than a 10% increase in grain size relative to their initial grain size.
After high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will form a continuous passive oxide layer thinner than 5 nm.
The combination of limited grain growth and a thin continuous oxide mitigates structural and chemical degradation during prolonged high-temperature operation.
Comparable lower-configurational-entropy nanoalloys typically undergo more pronounced grain coarsening under identical conditions.
Comparable lower-configurational-entropy nanoalloys typically form thicker, less protective, and less uniform oxide scales under identical conditions.
The proposed stability advantage applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic nanoalloys with grain sizes no greater than 50 nm at temperatures up to approximately 900 °C.
At substantially higher temperatures or markedly non-equiatomic compositions, the sluggish-diffusion and oxide-protection advantages may diminish.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes intrinsically sluggish diffusion while also requiring rapid surface segregation and quick oxide formation. The explanation that slow diffusion permits selective segregation does not resolve how the required Al/Cr transport remains rapid enough under the same conditions.
